articles.title_orig: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.title_zh: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.content_orig:
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Parnell said the secretary of the US Army would set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title_orig: Coco Gauff condemns online racism after disputed China Open point
articles.title_zh: Coco Gauff condemns online racism after disputed China Open point
articles.content_orig:
Beijing — Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.
Gauff requested a video review, prompting some boos from the crowd, after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Sun, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.
"Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X . "The amount of racist comments/dms I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.
Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam champion ranked No. 4, went on to take control of the match on Monday.
"Xinran is (an) incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff added in another post.
Sun, who was given a wild card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss.
Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.
"I did not like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career," Gauff said. "It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

articles.title_orig: US, China Extend Trade Truce But Port Fees Pending
articles.title_zh: US, China Extend Trade Truce But Port Fees Pending
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying on Sept. 23 that the United States and China agreed to extend the “Busan Agreement” trade truce, the issue of port fees on Chinese-built vessels is not finalized.
The truce, which had been scheduled to expire Nov. 10, now will be extended two months to Jan. 10, 2027. The overall extension was announced as Chinese President Xi Jinping met in Washington D.C. with President Donald Trump.
The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) still needs to issue an official Federal Register notice, which is required to legally bind the port fee postponement.
The California Chamber of Commerce joined more than 200 federal and state trade associations who sent a letter to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative , arguing that port fees on China-built vessels are not reviving U.S. shipbuilding and urging the Trump administration to extend their suspension.
“Vessel fees alone are not a strategy for rebuilding the U.S. shipbuilding industry,” wrote the signatories, which span the retail, agriculture, manufacturing and logistics sectors and include the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.
“Resuming vessel fees at this time would add another cost layer to an already-strained transportation system,” states the letter. “The costs would ripple across shipping networks, affect vessel deployment decisions, and increase uncertainty for businesses that have limited ability to control the ownership, operation, or construction history of the vessels used to transport their goods.”
The USTR opened a spring 2024 investigation at the request of the United Steelworkers and four other unions, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as a way to rebuild the U.S. shipbuilding industry.
A January 2025 USTR 182-page report detailed the decline of U.S. shipbuilding and U.S. flag carriers, and highlighted the dramatic expansion of China’s shipbuilding and ship operating sectors due to massive subsidies and preferential treatment.
Proposed remedies included significant “port service fees” against Chinese-built ships every time they enter a U.S. port. The fee also would have applied to operators with Chinese-built vessels in their fleet or having Chinese-built vessels on order. The remedy further included a requirement for U.S. exporters to export a certain percentage of goods on vessels owned, operated and eventually built in the United States.
There was a mix of support and opposition to the proposed remedies, which would have resulted in fees ranging from $1 million to $3 million — even as high as $3.5 million per port call. Unions and steel makers were supportive of the remedies, while carriers, shippers and farm exporters were strongly opposed.
However, a March 2025 study assessing the probable net economic effects of the proposed remedies found that overall, total exports and imports would decline, which would have a negative impact on the U.S. economy while the administration is striving to grow the overall economy and create jobs around the country.
All agreed that China’s dominance of the shipping industry should be addressed as the United States has lost more than 70,000 jobs in the last few decades and now ranks 19th globally in shipbuilding. Further, while China builds more than 1,000 ocean vessels for commercial use per year, the United States produces fewer than 10.
Originally the United States was to begin imposing new shipping fees in October 2025 that could have increased the cost of Chinese goods and potentially reduced imports. The Trump administration then agreed to pause the fees for a one-year period that would have ended Nov.10, 2026 before the latest extension to Jan. 10, 2027.

articles.title_zh: World War II: A New Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress
articles.content_orig:
A new World War II Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress supports teachers, librarians, and students in examining the people, places, and events of the war through primary sources from the Library’s digital collections. The eighteen-source set features newspapers, photographs, posters, maps, oral histories, letters, and other materials created during the period. A background essay provides historical context, teaching ideas, and links to additional Library of Congress resources.
These sources offer opportunities to explore some of the central questions and experiences of World War II from multiple perspectives. Americans contributed to the war effort as soldiers and civilians, workers and volunteers, and community members.
We hope this new source set will both be a useful and insightful way to explore World War II through the voices, images, and experiences preserved in the Library of Congress collections, and inspire students’ further inquiry and deeper investigation.

articles.title_orig: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.title_zh: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.content_orig:
British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.
The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub.
Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips.
British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines , last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft.
Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase.
The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.
Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.
British Airways' overhaul of its 12 A380s cabins are also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.

articles.title_orig: State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war
articles.title_zh: State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war
articles.content_orig:
Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthrough
Europe live – latest updates
Alternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war.
Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast.
Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy.
The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency, won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month , dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU).
Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained.
The AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority. Five politicians from the BSW, a small leftwing party that echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration, had already said they would vote for Rausch. Tuesday’s result means that four other MPs voted for the 35-year-old in the secret ballot.
The willingness of politicians to break the “firewall” – a moral agreement among other parties to shun the AfD – gives the party a chance of being able to form a government in the state – a feat it had looked unlikely to pull off. This would be even more of a historical watershed in postwar Germany.
The BSW’s support for Rausch came after the party’s founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, declared it was time to do away with “firewall idiocy”. The party’s deputy leader, Christian Leye, said the “firewall is not working” and the votes of nearly 44% of electors could not be ignored.
“We need an intelligent way of dealing with the AfD and that means dealing with the content of their programme instead of a firewall,” Leye told German media.
It was not immediately clear who was behind Tillschneider’s election because the BSW had said it would refuse to vote for him. He received 44 votes.
As the architect of the AfD’s “radical” manifesto, he is lined up to become culture and science minister in the state. He has referred to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as “a real man with a sound set of values” and accused immigrants of “streaming in here in masses … wanting to squander our money”.
Tillschneider is a scholar of Islamic studies who has described Islam as a “fungus” growing on the “German oak”. His family emigrated from Romania to Germany in the 1980s.
In his acceptance speech, Rausch promised to represent all voices and “take different opinions seriously and to try to take decisions in a transparent way”. He was applauded by his own parliamentary group and the ranks of the BSW. The other MPs did not respond.
after newsletter promotion
Rausch was one of the key figures in a nepotism scandal over AfD MPs employing family members in parliament. He denied claims that several of his siblings and a brother-in-law were working in the state parliament but confirmed he was employing several players from the football club where he is a member.
He is a close ally and confidant of Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, who is positioning himself to take over as leader of Saxony-Anhalt. He has yet to say which parties or politicians have agreed to cooperate with the AfD, only that “negotiations are going well”. The AfD claims to be courting members of the CDU to break the firewall, a claim CDU leaders deny.
The BSW says it will support an AfD-led parliament only if a nonpartisan figure is appointed to lead it, a position the AfD rejects. Siegmund has until December to form a government.
Opposition MPs raised alarm over the breaching of the firewall. “Whoever has invested a representative of extremist and anti-constitutional party with this office will bear responsibility for the consequences,” said Green MP Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, to loud applause.
The result of the Saxony-Anhalt poll, along with two other regional elections in September, has piled huge pressure on Merz, who pledged on taking office in 2025 that he would halve the AfD’s support by boosting the economy and reducing immigration. Instead, the CDU’s support has more or less halved and that of the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls.
Before the vote, Eva von Angern of the leftwing Die Linke party and the longest-serving member of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament, drew parallels between Rausch’s election to the post of speaker, and Hermann Göring’s use of that role in the Reichstag in the 1930s to facilitate Adolf Hitler’s rise to power.
She claimed that the negative consequences of the AfD’s win in the state were already being felt in lower tourist numbers and teachers withdrawing job applications.

articles.title_orig: Mark Mortimer, 'Another World' soap star, dies at 59
articles.title_zh: Mark Mortimer, 'Another World' soap star, dies at 59
articles.content_orig:
Mark Mortimer, best known for his role in the soap opera "Another World" in the '90s, died after "a fearless journey with cancer." He was 59 years old.
Mortimer died on Sept. 23, according to his obituary .
"He was an Army veteran, a model, an actor, an entrepreneur and a builder. He was a husband, father, son, brother and friend," his obituary said. "He was curious and determined, willing to take chances, start something new, change direction and figure things out along the way.
"But of all the titles Mark held throughout his life, the two that mattered most to him were husband and dad."
He acted in 81 episodes of "Another World" as Nick Hudson, appearing on the show from 1996 until the show's end in 1999, Variety and People reported.
He was first diagnosed with cancer in 2024. After that, he and his wife, Christie, founded the Integrative Access Foundation .
"Throughout Mark's journey, we met countless others who wanted more options but didn’t know where to turn, couldn’t afford the care, or were told their questions didn’t belong in traditional settings. The gap was clear, and it was deeply personal," according to the Integrative Access Foundation website. "Integrative Access was born from this experience."
Mortimer is survived by his wife, his daughter, Hunter, as well as his parents and several siblings.

The moves higher were bolstered by a rise in chipmakers. Shares of Marvell Technology popped 7%, while others such as Nvidia and Broadcom traded up around 1% and 4%, respectively.
Additionally, the benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield fell more than 4 basis points at 5.262%, while the 30-year bond yield declined more than 3 basis points to 5.631%. Both scaled to levels not seen since 2002 on Monday.
Bonds have been volatile over the past six weeks, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management investment chief Lisa Shalett said in a note to clients. She cited a potentially new Fed policy framework, economic growth and high oil prices while the Middle East conflict stretches on as factors.
"Nevertheless, while intraday implied volatility has risen, the six-week stretch has not reached the extremes that catalyzed the 2022 equity bear market," Shalett wrote.
Traders are now looking ahead to the Federal Reserve's minutes from its September meeting due Wednesday, which could shed some light on policymakers' move to raise rates.
Alongside Treasury yields, a drop in oil prices also gave equities a boost Tuesday. Brent crude traded 1% lower at around $99 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures shed less than 1% to roughly $88 a barrel.
Wall Street is getting more bullish on SpaceX.
Analyst Eric Sheridan at Goldman Sachs put a $230 price target and a buy rating on the stock in a Monday note to clients, implying upside of 44.7%.
He thinks the company is set to make more money from its artificial intelligence divisions than Wall Street currently expects.
"AI segment estimates still look relatively conservative (relative to Street estimates) over the next 6 to 18 months absent a correction across the broader AI operating landscape," he wrote.
Small-cap stocks underperformed on Tuesday as the three major averages saw sizable gains.
The Russell 2000 index was last trading just above the flatline, while the S&P 500 rose 0.8%. The Nasdaq Composite, which hit a new record high alongside the S&P 500 during the session, was higher by 0.8% as well, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 338 points, or 0.7%.
David Ellison's Paramount Skydance closed on its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery Tuesday, putting an end to a year-long takeover struggle that eventually entangled the future of film and television production in southern California, CBS News, CNN and settlement of a suit by attorneys generals from 12 states.
The new, successor company is named Skydance Corp. and, like its predecessor, trades on Nasdaq under ticker SKYD. Skydance joins two of the most stories film studios in Hollywood history, Paramount and Warner Brothers, as well as control of some one-third of basic cable programming .
Skydance shares fell another 2% in early trading Tuesday, bringing its 12-month loss to 50%.
— Scott Schnipper and Catriona Marangi
Bond yields may peak in the next month, Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote Tuesday, citing "several forces" that suggest a top between now and early November, among them the increased odds of some sort of resolution in the Middle East ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S.
Other signals include the move by the U.S. and European allies to release additional oil supplies, putting further downward pressure on crude oil prices, and harm being inflicted on the housing and auto industries by higher interest rates.
Slok said that 84% of global fixed income now yields more than 3%, "up from just 12% in January 2022."  Any deal "or government action that lowers oil prices would ease the upward pressure on interest rates at a time when yields are already elevated across nearly the entire global bond market," he said.
David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research in Toronto, a former chief North American economist at Merrill Lynch, said bond pressures are easing Tuesday as oil prices fall another 1% and European bond prices rally, noting that earlier in the day benchmark yields on Italian government debt dropped 11 basis points to 4.52%, in France by 10 bps to 4.76% and in the U.K. by 6 bps to 5.36%.
Shares of Marvell Technology jumped more than 7% in morning trading on Tuesday after the company provided long-term revenue guidance at its Investor Day.
Marvell expects its revenue for fiscal 2028 to come in at $20 billion, above the $18.17 billion that analysts polled by FactSet were looking for.
Looking out even further, the company sees its revenue being between $70 billion and $90 billion in fiscal 2031. That's well above the consensus estimate of $47.04 billion.
The latest move in the stock puts its year-to-date surge at more than 242%.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite traded at record levels on Tuesday morning.
The broad market index rose 0.5% shortly after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 189 points, or 0.4%.
If the S&P 500 ends the day above 7,798.99, it would post a new record close.

The U.S. trade deficit widened to levels not seen since before President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement early last year.
The deficit came in at $105.6 billion in August, the Commerce Department reported Tuesday. That's the largest amount since March 2025, when the deficit was at $132.98 billion, and was above the $102 billion that economists polled by the Dow Jones expected.
The dollar index also hit its low of the session at 101.754, marking its lowest level since Oct. 2, when the index hit a low of 101.668

The companies will pay $32.05 per share in cash, reflecting a total enterprise value of approximately $5.8 billion.
At the closing of the transaction, CD&R will hold a majority ownership interest, while McKesson will hold a minority ownership interest. Option Care Health will remain a separate entity with its own management team.
The transaction aligns with McKesson's strategic objectives, increasing its exposure to specialty and outpatient care, areas that have become increasingly important as more complex treatments shift outside hospitals.

articles.title_orig: AI companies stop short of guaranteeing agents will always obey safeguards
articles.title_zh: AI companies stop short of guaranteeing agents will always obey safeguards
articles.content_orig:
In the late 1990s, hundreds of internet companies suddenly appeared in New York City, many of them finding a home in Midtown South. Wall Street boomed, taking companies like Amazon.com and Pets.com public as their stocks soared.
But it didn’t last. When investors realized that the tech boom was a bubble, they abandoned the sector. The Nasdaq composite index plunged by 75% between March 2000 and October 2002. Investment dried up, and the vast majority of New York internet companies, like Pets.com, disappeared.
Even more dire, Wall Street contracted as profits plunged by two-thirds. It jettisoned some 35,000 jobs, or one in every four employees. The city’s finances, worsened by the costs of dealing with the 9/11 terrorist attacks, were so bad that Mayor Michael Bloomberg broke a campaign promise and pushed through a property tax increase.
The question in New York today is whether history is about to repeat itself.
Hundreds of artificial intelligence startups are putting down roots in New York , many in Midtown South, to take advantage of the city’s enormous talent pool and status as a global business center. The two most important companies — Anthropic and OpenAI — are building up their operations in what are likely to be their largest offices outside their San Francisco headquarters.
Just like two decades ago, Wall Street is booming, raising money for AI companies and prospering as investors send the stocks of those companies soaring. As a result, the securities industry is supporting the city’s economy and generating billions of dollars to cover up big problems in both the state’s and city’s budgets.
“New York City has ridden the AI boom more than anyone in America except San Francisco,” City Comptroller Mark Levine said. “We are financing the data center construction boom; our firms are running the initial public offerings.
“But New Yorkers don’t realize how our fate has been tied to the AI boom,” he added. “It’s not like San Francisco, where people who work for tech companies are the most prominent figures. Here it’s a step removed.”
A bubble is when asset prices, like stocks or homes, increase so rapidly that they no longer reflect their fundamental value based on the profits they can generate. Could that be true for AI companies’ valuations today? As a recent Wall Street Journal article — “ How to Know When the AI Boom Is About to Go Bust ” — indicates, that’s the question on everyone’s mind.
New York City would feel the tremors almost immediately if Wall Street reels after an AI implosion.
“AI is [the] No. 1 earnings driver for big banks this year,” well-known Wall Street expert Mike Mayo told Yahoo Finance . “The capital demands from tech firms, utilities and related industries amounts to a 100-foot wave lifting Wall Street.”
The $25 billion securities firms earned in the second quarter of this year is 66% higher than what they earned in the same period a year ago. The $46 billion generated in the first six months of 2026 is 50% higher than in the same period in 2025 and is already two-thirds of the way to beating 2025’s record earnings. That $46 billion is also more than what the city’s budget assumes such firms will earn for the entire year.
Wall Street profits this year are “stunning,” according to the monthly economic newsletter from Levine’s office.
That wave lifts the state budget, where 20% of all revenue comes from Wall Street. The securities industry provides 9% of all city tax revenue, and when the state budget is flush, Albany can send more money to the city, which Hochul did this year with an additional $4 billion.
In 2001, tax revenues dropped by 5% when Wall Street contracted, according to the fiscal watchdog Citizens Budget Commission. The city had been planning on an increase in tax revenue, so when the dot-com bubble burst, a giant hole opened in the city’s budget.
Today, the Mamdani administration is already projecting a $6 billion budget gap for 2028. A 5% decline in revenue would turn that into a whopping $10 billion hole that would create the city’s worst budget crisis in more than a decade.
Levine told The City Reporter that the dangers posed by a Wall Street contraction are why he has consistently argued the city’s budget reserves are inadequate.
The Mamdani administration declined to comment on what an AI contraction and Wall Street plunge would mean for the city.
Even the biggest beneficiaries know the boom will end at some point.
“It’s getting close to as good as it gets,” JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon said in July as the bank announced the largest quarterly profit any bank had ever produced. (JPMorganChase is a corporate sponsor of The City Reporter).
“We’re in a very healthy, active, exuberant market with very high prices and very high volumes,” he said. “We just don’t know how long it will continue.”
No one knows how severe an AI contraction will be. But many are worried. Michael Burry, a key character in Michael Lewis’ book “The Big Short” who foresaw the housing collapse and financial crisis of 2008, has said a collapse on a similar scale is coming sooner rather than later . Many are focused on this boom’s circular financing where Nvidia, the key supplier of AI chips, is also financing its customers. Nvidia has said it is solid enough financially to do this, but others doubt it.
Even if some AI companies disappear, many of their employees may have options, unlike workers hit by the dot-com bubble.
“It won’t be fun,” said Julie Samuels, CEO of the local industry trade group Tech:NYC. “The financial firms will sweep up the best engineers even if there is a downturn on Wall Street.”
Optimists like Cornell Tech Dean Greg Morrisett are unsettled by the parallels to the dot-com bubble but remain confident about the future.
“You get worried about a big reset,” he said. “I think it’s very analogous to the early 2000 with overhyped companies, like Pets.com , and froth in the markets, overhyping and underdelivering.”
But, he added, “Out of that emerged companies like Google,” which is the largest tech employer in New York, with about 10,000 workers.

Ticket demand for the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup 2027 has surged past the one-million mark, with more than one million applications submitted in less than three days since the ticket ballot opened on 1 October 2026.
Over 320,000 fans have already registered for the ballot, submitting applications for matches across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia as anticipation continues to build for the 14th edition of the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup.
The India vs Pakistan fixture on 10 October is currently attracting the highest demand, with more than 100,000 ticket applications received. South Africa vs India follows with more than 86,000 applications, while India vs Australia has attracted more than 80,000.
The pre-seeded Super 7 fixture between India (A1) and Pakistan (A3) on 7 November has received almost 75,000 applications, making it the fourth most in-demand match. The 21 November Final has also proved popular , with almost 65,000 applications already submitted.
The tournament will feature 14 of the world’s best teams , with the first ball set to be bowled on 2 October and the Final scheduled for 21 November.
With excitement building across the three host nations, the ICC has opened the ticket ballot to give fans around the world the opportunity to register for a chance to attend the tournament.
Breaking down the new Cricket World Cup format | CWC27
A new format awaits at the 2027 Cricket World Cup!  
Crystal Arnold takes us through what to expect as South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia prepare to co-host the tournament.
Ticket prices range from USD $9.62 (R158) for entry-level tickets to USD $31.31 (R514) for the highest-tier matches. Special consideration has also been given to family bundles, student and pensioner pricing, early-bird local allocations, and community club and school group pricing.
ICC CEO, Sanjog Gupta said: “One million ticket applications in just over 48 hours of opening the ticket ballot is a demonstration of the attention, stature and affiliation for ICC Cricket World Cup 2027. ICC events are now spectacles which transcend cultural and geographic boundaries and serve as platforms to widen and deepen fandom for the sport.
“This is also Africa's moment to shine as an ICC marquee men's event is returning to the continent after two decades and brings with it the attention of 2.5 billion cricket fans across 120+ countries. We aim to ‘make the circle bigger’, for fans, for the athletes, for the game, and for communities who will gather to celebrate the competition and the culture. The ballot is open, and we can't wait to host the world so get in if you haven't already.”
Fans have until 23h59 (CAT) on 21 November to register for the ballot and select their desired matches at tickets.cricketworldcup.com .

articles.title_orig: Man living in Congo who returned to Kenya is country's first confirmed Ebola case and first death
articles.title_zh: Man living in Congo who returned to Kenya is country's first confirmed Ebola case and first death
articles.content_orig:
Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.
This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.
A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.
The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.
Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.
Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.
He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).
Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.
He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.
Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.
Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.
After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.
The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.
The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.
“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”
The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.
Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”
North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Jacob Kiplimo, at just 25-years-old, has had one of the best seasons in running history - and on Sunday, he could cap that off with a win and World Record at the 2026 Chicago Marathon .
Kiplimo currently holds a personal best of 2:00:28 over the full marathon distance, and he also has the half marathon World Record of 57:20 to his name - but more on that soon.
Australian, British, Irish and Canadian audiences can watch the Chicago Marathon LIVE on FloTrack
The Ugandan has had an unbelievable season so far in 2026. It all started at the 2026 World XC Championships where Kiplimo collected his third World XC Title in-a-row . He gapped Berihu Aregawi to win by 18-seconds in a statement victory.
Kiplimo then headed to Portugal in March. At the Lisbon Half Marathon, the young star set a World Record in the Half Marathon by posting a 57:20 for a 48-second victory.
Just over a month later, Kiplimo ran the 2026 London Marathon. In just his third race at the distance he finished third with an astounding 2:00:28. That race saw Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha run the two fastest times in World History.
But now - it may be Kiplimo's opportunity to raise the laurels in the Windy City.
It will be his first race since London - and the only thing holding him back may be the weather.
Conditions are expected to be a little warmer than expected for a mid-October race. Currently, temperatures are calling for Mid-60's, climbing up to the high 60's by the projected finish time around 9:30 AM. Humidity expected to be in the 50% to 60% range.
These conditions are outside of the optimal ranges for marathon running - but Kiplimo can certainly still prevail.
Amos Kipruto will stand as one of the toughest competitors in Sunday's field. Of Kenya, the 34 year old ran 2:01:39 to finish fourth behind Kiplimo at the 2026 London Marathon.
Kipruto has been a consistent contender on the World Major Marathon circuit this decade. He won London in 2022 and has sat on five World Major Podiums.
He is on a hot-streak in Chicago too. In 2024 his 2:04:50 earned him a third-place finish. Then in 2025 he upgraded to silver with a 2:03:54 effort.
Ethiopia's Milkesa Mengesha and Tadese Takele Bikila will also be in the mix. They both sport personal bests in the low-2:03's.
You also can't count out the Americans. Tough conditions could open the race up for Charles Hicks, Vinny Mauri, or Clayton Young. All will be gunning for the American Record of 2:04:43, which could spell an opportunity for an American to dip into the 2:03's.

articles.title_orig: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage, disclosing state secrets and attempted treason
articles.title_zh: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage, disclosing state secrets and attempted treason
articles.content_orig:
Police have arrested the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency , August Hanning, on suspicion of espionage, the federal prosecutor's office announced Tuesday.
Hanning served as the agency's chief from December 1998 to November 2005 before moving to the Federal Interior Ministry, where he worked as state secretary until November 2009.
According to a statement from the prosecutor's office, the 80-year-old faces charges including espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason and working as a secret service agent.
It did not say which foreign intelligence service he is suspected of working for.
The statement added that another former high-ranking BND employee was also arrested on suspicion of providing hundreds of classified documents to Hanning after his tenure as spy chief ended in exchange for payment.
DW's chief political editor Michaela Küfner, reporting from a government press briefing on the arrest, described the case as Germany's "biggest espionage scandal of the century."
Police arrested Hanning early Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde near the western German city of Münster, according to information from WDR, NDR and the daily Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Hanning's alleged accomplice, who was identified only as Manfred D. in line with Germany's privacy laws, was taken into custody in Bavaria.
Authorities were conducting searches at both suspects' properties, as well as in Berlin, the prosecutor said.
During Hanning's tenure as spy head, D. served as his chief of staff. He also subsequently worked under Hanning at the Interior Ministry until 2009.
He is facing charges of "aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state."
Marc Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament's intelligence oversight committee, said following the arrests that Germany "will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets."
"Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out," he said in comments to the AFP news agency.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, also a member of the oversight committee, said the allegations were "deeply troubling" and called for a "swift and thorough investigation."
The investigation into Hanning reportedly began due to his connection to a high-profile trial involving businesswoman Christine Block.

The prosecutor's office said Hanning and Manfred D. are believed to have come up with their arrangement in 2010.
From 2012 to March 2026, D. served as chief of staff to Hanning's successors at the BND spy agency, where he had access to a wealth of classified documents, according to the prosecutor's statement.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement said.
It added that D. is alleged to have provided Hanning with information until at least mid-2022, and that Hanning used that information in his private consulting work.
"In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service," Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor's office, told German broadcaster RTL.
The prosecutor's statement said Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years."
Hanning and D. are expected to appear before an investigating judge on Tuesday and Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: XtalPi Debuts Kodexia™, the World's First Closed-Loop siRNA Platform Combining Generative AI with First-Principles Modeling
articles.title_zh: XtalPi Debuts Kodexia™, the World's First Closed-Loop siRNA Platform Combining Generative AI with First-Principles Modeling
articles.content_orig:
BOSTON and BEIJING , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XtalPi Holdings Limited (HKEX: 2228), an AI and robotics-driven drug and materials discovery company, today debuted Kodexia™, the industry's first closed-loop small interfering RNA (siRNA) discovery platform combining generative AI, first-principles-driven biological modeling, and automated experimentation. Validating the rapid execution capabilities of this new infrastructure, the company simultaneously announced the advancement of six proprietary therapeutic programs, marking the successful expansion of XtalPi's technology into nucleic acid therapeutics.
By silencing disease-driving genes upstream of protein production, siRNA therapeutics offer immense potential for biological targets that conventional modalities struggle to address. However, clinical development remains heavily constrained by fragmented sequence and modification design processes, restrictive patent barriers, inconsistent translation from cellular assays to animal models, and severe limitations in extrahepatic delivery.
To address these interdependent bottlenecks, XtalPi drew on domain-specific expertise to develop siFormer, the proprietary architecture at the core of Kodexia™. By seamlessly integrating RNAi biological mechanisms with nucleic acid chemistry principles, siFormer delivers a qualitative leap in predictive accuracy that surpasses conventional design baselines. The architecture incorporates RNA thermodynamics and structural features relevant to strand loading, target accessibility, and silencing efficiency. These mechanistic constraints guide molecular generation toward biologically plausible designs rather than relying on sequence correlations alone. Through this unified approach, Kodexia™ enables researchers to systematically balance potency, in vivo translation, durability, off-target activity, safety, and patentability instead of optimizing single endpoints in isolation.
To execute this multiparameter optimization, XtalPi utilizes a closed-loop process of computational design, automated experimentation, and empirical feedback. Generative models and the proprietary siFormer architecture operate continuously with XtalPi's automated laboratories, which conduct more than 500 in vitro and 30 in vivo experiments weekly. This seamless integration enables the parallel development of multiple target programs, yielding a nearly threefold increase in design efficiency. Notably, more than 50% of first-round designs tested across multiple programs showed stronger in vivo activity than positive controls.
Kodexia™ also globally co-optimizes dual-target siRNAs as single molecules, creating a strategy for disease biology that may not be adequately addressed through single-target intervention. For extrahepatic delivery, the platform co-designs siRNA molecules with their targeting systems and applies multi-objective optimization to antibody, peptide, and small-molecule conjugates. These capabilities are being applied to delivery research targeting the kidney, spleen, and adipose tissue.
The platform's lead program in immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy serves as an early empirical validation of this unified architecture. articles.title_orig: Will the system in the Gulf impact the US? See spaghetti models
articles.title_zh: Will the system in the Gulf impact the US? See spaghetti models
articles.content_orig:
Tropical Storm Isaias is likely to form and may target parts of the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to Florida, before spreading soaking rain inland through the Southeast this weekend.
An area of low pressure, tagged Invest 92L by the National Hurricane Center, has formed off the coast of eastern Mexico in the southwestern Gulf. Invests are tagged when the NHC is interested in running specialized computer models on a system and want to send the hurricane hunters to investigate.
The National Hurricane Center has tentatively scheduled the first hurricane hunter mission into this system for Wednesday afternoon.
During the next couple days, it will be in an environment that appears at least somewhat favorable for formation, which could happen as soon as Wednesday or Thursday.
If it becomes a tropical storm (a low pressure system with a well-defined, closed-off center and sustained winds of at least 39 mph), it would be called Tropical Storm Isaias (ees-ah-EE-ahs), which would be the ninth storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
(MORE: Hurricane season maps tracker )
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
There are various model forecast tracks that range from the upper Texas coast to the Florida Panhandle, with more of them beginning to trend closer to the Florida Panhandle.
Rain chances will be on the increase by Friday in that region and widespread rainfall is likely this weekend across the Southeast.
This means additional rain for the already soaked Southeast and Gulf Coast, especially along and to the east of the track of this system.
Heavy rainfall can occur well inland, which can lead to flooding for people not as used to heavy tropical moisture. Also, should heavy rain fall across higher elevation areas, landslides could be possible.
( Hurricane preparedness: What you need to know during hurricane season )
With the jet stream sagging far to the south, this system may have to battle wind shear along the northern Gulf.
You can see the wind shear forecast below; the colors in darker purple and white indicate strong shear. Wind shear disrupts, weakens and sometimes entirely prevents the development of tropical systems and hurricanes.
However, if the jet stream shifts a little farther north, there could be a window of opportunity for more strengthening. That will be something we have to watch closely in the coming days.
It is likely that this system will be weakening closer to landfall, if this system comes northward through the Gulf.
If you're near the Gulf Coast, from Texas to Florida, monitor the latest forecast for this system and have your hurricane plans ready to go, just in case.
Despite one of the least active hurricane seasons in years, that doesn't mean an impactful storm can't happen this late in the season.
And it doesn't take a hurricane to trigger major rainfall flooding, as we saw earlier this season with Tropical Storm Arthur's flooding in the South.
(MORE: Stay prepared this hurricane season )
While El Niño continues to shred some systems before they form and weaken the ones that do, three storms have battled the conditions to actually get names and impact the Gulf Coast states. These storms may have not been hurricanes, but they did bring heavy rainfall to the region.
All systems like this one need is a window of an opportunity with relatively less wind shear, even in El Niño-assisted conditions.
The tracks of Tropical Storms Arthur, Bertha and Edouard.
Tropical Storm Arthur was a brief June storm that quickly reached tropical storm strength right before a Texas landfall. The low fell apart quickly after moving onshore, but its remnants brought torrential rainfall over the Gulf Coast. Arthur actually brought 37.53 inches to Alexandria, Louisiana, which was the wettest rainfall total caused by an Atlantic tropical cyclone.
In July, Tropical Storm Bertha formed in the northeast quadrant of the Gulf.  It moved to the north before interestingly turning west and striking the Biloxi Wildlife Management Area in St. Bernard Parish Wednesday afternoon on July 22. Rainfall totals of 1-5 inches were widespread with isolated totals exceeding 5 inches.
The next storm to impact the Gulf was Tropical Storm Edouard, which made landfall on Sept. 1, 2026. Winds were around 60 mph at the time of landfall and heavy rainfall was also reported.
Even though this hurricane season has proved to be one of the quietest on record, that doesn’t mean we can’t get an impactful tropical system or hurricane.
There have been seasons in the past that have managed to produce strong storms despite a strong El Niño.

articles.title_orig: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
“That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution, which is less than half a page, says.
The measure is expected to be considered by the faculty senate, which meets Oct. 14, according to a statement from faculty senator Paul Ortiz.
“The goal is to really force systemic change,” Ortiz, a professor of labor history, said in a statement.
Ortiz added that “students have been telling us stories they don’t feel safe, and this has been going on for a number of years” and called the situation a “systemic problem.” He reiterated that the senate was not “targeting any individual” but that the students and faculty “have been unsatisfied with the response.”
“Women need to feel safe,” he said.
In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty they were “upset, fearful for their personal safety,” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus.
Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement added.
Cornell declined to comment.
The proposed no-confidence resolution marks an escalation in pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with the alleged sexual assault.
She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana.
The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days and prompted protests on the university’s campus after widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate the woman’s allegations.
Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days.
“If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.”
Brady said that Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing on the case to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.”
“If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.”
If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty and Cornell’s leadership for policies affecting sexual assault.
Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady says those recommendations have largely been ignored.
“If the administration came out and said: ‘you know what? we screwed up, we did A, B, and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said. “If they did that? That goes so far.”
Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca; Matt Lavietes reported from New York City.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

Googlebook is pitched as the laptop for Android users but, at launch, the vast majority of Android users can’t use the platform’s best features.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.

The organisers say some 100,000 people are taking part in the Paris demonstration, bringing up the national total to 450,000.
The French interior ministry’s figure is much lower: they say some 250,000 joined the protests, with 56,000 people reported in Paris.
In the last half hour the protests in Paris turned violent in parts of it as an estimated group of 300 people repeatedly clashed with the police.
The minister for Europe and foreign affairs, Jean-Noël Barrot, said “all our rivals, adversaries, partners, are trying to tell” the ongoing high school protests in France “in their own way.”
He was giving his reaction to comments by Donald Trump who claimed that “Islam” and “immigration” were factors behind the high school movement in France.
Many young people are trying to leave Place de la Nation through a police checkpoint where bag searches are being carried out, Liberation reported, with the unrest said to be gradually easing.
A police officer who fired a tear gas grenade into a student’s face has been charged.
The incident occurred in front of a high school in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône on September 28.
The officer has been charged with “violence by a person in a position of public authority resulting in mutilation or permanent disability ,” the Pontoise prosecutor’s office announced, Liberation reported.
Live footage from Place de la Nation in Paris shows growing tensions between a group of protesters and the police at the end of today’s manifestation, with officers firing tear gas to control the crowds.
I will keep an eye on that.
As if tensions were not high enough, US president Donald Trump has decided to wade in with his trademark mastery of nuance and deep understanding of French society.
Writing on Truth Social, he blamed the high school protests on “out of control mass migration” and “Islam wanting to take over a once great country.”
“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country! President DJT”
School students say the education system is riven with inequality, that many buildings are in disrepair, class sizes are too big, and there are not enough teachers or funding .
The French prime minister has promised to address what he called “legitimate” complaints, including on class sizes, long hours, dilapidated buildings and teacher provisions.
So how bad are French high schools and what are the main problems?
Is the French education system blighted by social inequality?
Yes. A child born and schooled in a deprived neighbourhood in France has less chance of escaping their socioeconomic background than in most other developed nations, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Éric Charbonnier, a French education analyst at the OECD, said there was a marked gap between the performance of the most advantaged and disadvantaged school students in France. “And often disadvantaged students are in disadvantaged schools,” he said. This has raised issues of the quality of learning being delivered and higher absenteeism of teachers.
Teachers’ unions and sociologists have said children in France are often segregated by their background, postcode and income, with a direct impact on education outcomes.
Are French high school buildings dilapidated and rat-infested with collapsing ceilings?
Some are, namely in certain cities and low-income suburbs. V ideos filmed by students and teachers have shown leaks, scurrying rats, holes in walls and ceilings, broken toilets and not enough chairs or tables, meaning teachers have to carry them from classroom to classroom. Some children said they had to learn in class while leaks were pouring into buckets, or move desks to avoid getting wet. Many school classrooms experienced temperatures over 35C (95F) in the heatwaves of last May and June.
Estimates in recent years have pointed to thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, in need of repair. These include many 1960s school buildings. French regions are responsible for upkeep of high school buildings, but have asked for higher budgets from the government. A senate report has advised that billions need to be spent in the coming years to renovate and repair schools, as well as to address the impact of the climate crisis.
Are class sizes bigger than other comparable countries?
Yes, and often in urban areas. Charbonnier said: “There are an average of 29 students in French language lessons, compared with 26 across the OECD. However, this average masks substantial differences – particularly between large cities and rural areas.”
Teachers and school students in Paris and its suburbs this week described many high school classes of 36 pupils or more , but in some rural areas it can be fewer. Figures from the French education ministry show class sizes have increased in recent years.
Does France spend less money on secondary education than its European neighbours?
No, France actually spends more than many other countries on high schools for children aged 15 and 18, but analysts question how the French government is spending its money and for what outcomes. For example, teachers’ middle and end-career salaries are comparatively low.

But there are also reports of some clashes with the police on the margins of the main march.
Let’s go back to France for the latest on the school protests.
Czech public broadcaster Česká televize said it would skip next year’s Eurovision song contest over spending cuts forced by a planned switch to financing from the state budget , AFP reported.

Critics, including the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) press watchdog, say the move jeopardises the independence of public media, and the media staged a token strike over the plan in June.

“Sweden is deploying the Patriot air defence system to Poland to strengthen the protection of Nato’s eastern flank. The Swedish forces will protect the logistics hub in south-eastern Poland that plays a key role in providing military and civilian support to Ukraine,” the Swedish armed forces said .

Vice President & Founder, Google Arts & Culture
Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder Athens

Artist Theo Triantafyllidis won this year’s Frieze Artist Award for his interactive sculpture, "Feral Metaverse (Spider)." This climbable, giant spider structure invites visitors to cooperate in both physical and digital gaming environments. You can see this collaborative project at Frieze London from October 14–18 or visit Google Arts & Culture to explore how the team used artificial intelligence to build it.
Artist Theo Triantafyllidis built a giant, climbable spider sculpture that doubles as a multiplayer video game. He worked with a huge team and used AI to help design the game’s look and digital world. Visitors have to help each other climb the spider to play, which encourages people to work together. It’s a cool way to show how art and technology can bring people closer.
Athens-based artist Theo Triantafyllidis is the recipient of this year’s Frieze Artist Award, which supports artists at pivotal moments in their careers as they create ambitious new work. Triantafyllidis works with video games, live simulations, performances, and physical installations to build playful worlds exploring complex phenomena. At Frieze London, he’ll present 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026,' a participatory climbable spider sculpture and live multiplayer game rooted in shared experiences.
In Triantafyllidis’ words, “spiders are the original engineers.” Strange, intelligent and unexpectedly tender, the spider became a central figure for an artwork built around physical contact, cooperation, and play.
Theo Triantafyllidis, Photo: Paris Tavitian, Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
From afar, the giant spider-shaped structure might appear intimidating, but up close, its softness invites touch. Visitors are encouraged to help one another climb the sculpture. Once players are aboard the legs, the experience extends into the Feral Metaverse, a shared digital environment where players collaborate, move, and form temporary collective bodies together.
Theo Triantafyllidis, 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026.' Game still. Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
The award allowed Triantafyllidis to expand his team of sculptors, fabricators, textile designers, game developers, and civil engineers. For this project, the group introduced Gemini into their workflow, working with it as a tool and collaborator as they generated the sketches, character designs, backdrops, and 3D renders that shaped the look and feel of the game. In rendering AI outputs as sculptural material, they were able to push both the game and the audience interaction with it.
The experience, which requires players to watch each other, exchange advice, and learn together, will move between the screen and the booth at Frieze. It’s a testament to how both public and online spaces can foster cooperation and warmth.

articles.title_orig: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come
articles.title_zh: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come
articles.content_orig:
CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.
Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive.
"I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.
Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential , questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next.
Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list .
Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity.
For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."
For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology.
"You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."
Ibrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.
Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:
That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said.
With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce .
"They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."
Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens."
"One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.

articles.title_orig: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.title_zh: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.content_orig:
By Jamie Durrani 2026-10-06T13:33:00+01:00
Source: © Nobel Prize Outreach/Niklas Elmehed
Francis Halzen is the first solo winner of the physics prize for more than 30 years
The 2026 Nobel prize in physics has been awarded to Belgian astrophysicist Francis Halzen for his work on the detection of high-energy cosmic neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy. Halzen spearheaded the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which has enabled scientists to track high-energy neutrinos that have reached Earth from the farthest reaches of the universe. It is the first time that the physics prize has been awarded to an individual recipient since 1992, when Georges Charpak was recognised for his work on particle detectors .
Neutrinos are elementary particles released by many different sources, including radioactive substances, the sun and other celestial bodies. But the neutrinos released by highly energetic processes like giant supernovae in the distant universe can have energies far higher than other cosmic neutrinos. As a result, these high-energy neutrinos – which have no charge and almost no mass – travel across the universe barely interacting with other matter and without changing direction or losing energy. This means that when these neutrinos reach the Earth they carry information about extreme environments in distant regions of space that cannot be gathered by monitoring other types of radiation such as light or gamma rays.
But the very properties that make high-energy cosmic neutrinos such useful carriers of information also make them incredibly difficult to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen came up with the idea of building a giant facility at the South Pole, where flashes of blue light given off as neutrinos pass through the Antarctic ice could be tracked. Halzen and his colleague John Learned presented the concept at a conference in Poland in June 1988.
Source: © Johan Jamestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
The IceCube neutrino observatory is a huge cubic kilometre of ice dotted with sensors that was the brainchild of Halzen
Since then, Halzen, who works at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, has spent years developing techniques to detect neutrinos, contributing to projects in Greenland and Antarctica that honed the technology. Eventually, he led an initiative that culminated in the construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, in which more than 5000 special sensors are spread across a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice deep below the surface.
The IceCube facility was completed in 2011, and uncovered the first evidence of high-energy cosmic neutrinos just two years later. The project involves more than 450 researchers from 14 countries and has paved the way for further international collaboration to detect cosmic neutrinos. Speaking at the prize announcement, the Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce noted that a global network of neutrino telescopes, based in ice and the oceans, is currently being established, which will allow researchers to ‘monitor all of the sky, all of the time’.
Speaking on the phone immediately after the announcement, Halzen described the award as ‘a great surprise’ and emphasised the critical contributions from his collaborators over the years. ‘When we started this project, everybody realised this was a good idea, but very few thought it would work – including myself,’ he said. ‘So this was an adventure where success was not guaranteed and we were lucky to overcome the various challenges, partly because the talent of collaborators and partly because of luck. It was a long journey, but it finally worked.’
