A new Radio World ebook considers trends in consoles and control surfaces. In this companion piece, Mark Ruddy takes our questions. He’s chief engineer at WVIA Public Media , covering Northeast and Central Pennsylvania.
Radio World: Mark, what do you consider the most important trend in the design of consoles and control surfaces for radio broadcast studios?
Mark Ruddy: It seems that consoles are trending as less of a hardware item, and more of a software item.
The shift to an on-screen console seems that it can work for some applications, but I am happy to see that innovations continue in hardware-based control surfaces. Being a radio station that operates with live personnel, they are familiar with the layout of a hardware-based console. The most important functions for me as an engineer are to see levels for a source that is loaded into a channel and for the surface to function reliably and accurately.
Even though control surfaces are trending smaller, it is good that options still remain for larger layouts and designs.
RW: What is the definition of a radio console now?
Ruddy: In most cases, it is akin to a keyboard for a computer. It is there and functions as a radio console, but really with other means to connect, it is less critical of a component for operation. The exception does exist still for analog or digital-based consoles, but when audio isn’t passing directly though the console, it’s more of an interface.
RW: How has their evolution changed the way engineers view them and plan around their installation?
Ruddy: The evolution of consoles into control surfaces has certainly made things more efficient and effective when planning installation. In most cases it is just running a network cable and power, with the audio entering the system through other means, the installation of a control surface is much neater and in the case of AoIP, it keeps wiring localized and minimizes cable runs.
RW: To what extent has scripting changed console operations, and what does scripting make possible?
Ruddy: Scripting allows for more under-the-hood tasks to be accomplished without anybody realizing what it is doing. Even by doing simple routes or logic controls, it’s very much more efficient.
If you have an automation system that integrates with your installation, it makes things even easier for an operator by being able to execute a hotkey and not having to worry about anything else.
RW: How vibrant is the marketplace for analog consoles?
Ruddy: I believe that there is still a need for analog consoles and will be. Some stations don’t need much more than that for their operations, and they are very useful for at-home studios. Current analog consoles make for a cost-effective upgrade for an aging console.
RW: Any suggested best practices or common errors to avoid when choosing one?
Ruddy: Just recognize your requirements, then make sure to research all available options. What is right for one operation isn’t necessarily right for another. There are many manufacturers making quality consoles and systems, but each one does have its pros and cons. I would also say to reach out to other stations or groups who are using the system you’re looking at to get their opinion and run questions by them as well. That was invaluable for me in choosing our current system.

articles.title_orig: Whistleblower says Trump demanded FBI probe into protesters over a TikTok he saw
articles.title_zh: Whistleblower says Trump demanded FBI probe into protesters over a TikTok he saw
articles.content_orig:
The FBI opened preliminary investigations targeting anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement protesters in Southern California, a former FBI intelligence official alleged in a whistleblower complaint, adding that she believed the move violated the law and agency policy.
The investigations were opened in early 2025 in the early weeks of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown following demands from President Donald Trump and other administration officials, according to the disclosure by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office.
CNN reviewed the complaint, which was filed by lawyers representing Fields to members of the Senate Judiciary Committee.
A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN said the DOJ will continue to “vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law.”
“The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job.”
A statement from the White House also suggested the investigation was focused on violent acts, which it said are not protected by the First Amendment.
“These allegations are FALSE. The First Amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
CNN has also reached out to the FBI for comment.
In at least one instance, the FBI began preliminary investigations of protesters after the president demanded an investigation of people he saw in a TikTok video depicting demonstrators against ICE and Customs and Border Protection in Alhambra, California. The protesters were using bullhorns to warn neighbors about the presence of immigration-enforcement officers, Fields’ disclosure said.
Following the February 2025 protest in Alhambra, an analyst who worked under Fields “informed her that the squad had been ordered to run pre‑assessment checks on the two to four anti‑ICE and CBP protesters in the video accused of impeding an immigration arrest, even though FBI policy prohibits opening investigations based solely on First Amendment‑protected activity, and the squad did not yet have evidence of a crime,” lawyers representing Fields said in a letter to senators.
The investigations came after FBI Director Kash Patel told top FBI leaders that the president “was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested,” the letter said.
In a letter to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, citing the whistleblower complaint, Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla questioned the Justice Department on how many investigations into protestors were currently active and whether Trump had directed other, similar investigations.
Massive crowds turn out at anti-ICE protests across the US
Fields’ whistleblower complaint disclosed two separate incidents in which she said White House officials demanded the FBI investigate and arrest anti-ICE protesters.
A separate incident weeks earlier sparked a similar focus on free speech, according to Fields, when then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove demanded the FBI investigate a group of anti-ICE protestors outside a federal building in California.
In both cases, Fields noted that First Amendment protections prohibited such investigations and potential charges unless other action beyond speech had taken place.
When she raised the issue with one superior, Fields says she was told it had to happen.
The former analyst said she was stripped of her team and lost support from FBI leadership in her Los Angeles office, pushing her to ultimately resign from the bureau.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
articles.title_zh: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
articles.content_orig:
Scientists have identified a way to restore cartilage in aging knee joints, at least in mice, by blocking a protein whose levels rise with age. The approach not only reversed naturally occurring cartilage loss in older animals, but also protected mice from developing arthritis after knee injuries similar to ACL tears in people.
The findings also showed promise in human tissue. Cartilage samples collected during knee replacement surgeries responded to the treatment by beginning to produce new, functional cartilage.
Together, the results suggest that cartilage damaged by aging or arthritis may be more capable of repair than previously thought. If the strategy ultimately works in people, researchers believe it could potentially lead to an oral medicine or injection that regenerates cartilage and reduces the need for knee or hip replacement surgery.
Targeting the damage behind osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease in which cartilage gradually breaks down, leaving joints painful, swollen and increasingly difficult to move. It affects about one in five adults in the United States and is estimated to account for roughly $65 billion in direct health care costs each year.
Current treatments mainly focus on controlling pain and other symptoms. Once the disease becomes severe, replacing the damaged joint surgically may be the only remaining option. There is currently no drug that can reliably slow or reverse osteoarthritis itself.
The Stanford Medicine-led study instead focused on a protein called 15-PGDH. The researchers have described it as a gerozyme, a term for enzymes that become more abundant with age and contribute to the gradual loss of tissue function.
Previous work by the same group showed that 15-PGDH acts as an important regulator of aging in multiple tissues. Blocking the protein with a small molecule increased muscle mass and endurance in old mice. Doing the opposite, increasing 15-PGDH in young animals, caused their muscles to shrink and weaken. The protein has also been linked to the regeneration of bone, nerve and blood cells.
In many of those tissues, healing depends on tissue-specific stem cells multiplying and developing into specialized cells. Cartilage turned out to behave differently. Instead of relying on stem cells, existing cartilage cells called chondrocytes changed their patterns of gene activity and shifted toward a more youthful state.
"This is a new way of regenerating adult tissue, and it has significant clinical promise for treating arthritis due to aging or injury," said Helen Blau, PhD, professor of microbiology and immunology. "We were looking for stem cells, but they are clearly not involved. It's very exciting."
Blau, who directs the Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology and is the Donald E. and Delia B. Baxter Foundation Professor, and Nidhi Bhutani, PhD, associate professor of orthopaedic surgery, are the senior authors of the research, which was published in Science . Instructor of orthopedic surgery Mamta Singla, PhD, and former postdoctoral scholar Yu Xin (Will) Wang, PhD, are the lead authors of the study. Wang is now an assistant professor at the Sanford Burnham Institute in San Diego.
"Dramatic regeneration" of cartilage
"Millions of people suffer from joint pain and swelling as they age," Bhutani said. "It is a huge unmet medical need. Until now, there has been no drug that directly treats the cause of cartilage loss. But this gerozyme inhibitor causes a dramatic regeneration of cartilage beyond that reported in response to any other drug or intervention."
Cartilage is not all the same. The human body contains three major types, each designed for a different job.
Elastic cartilage is soft and flexible and helps form structures such as the outer ear. Fibrocartilage is tougher and better suited to absorbing force, including in areas between the vertebrae of the spine. Hyaline cartilage is smooth and slippery, allowing bones to move against one another with very little friction in joints such as the ankles, hips, shoulders and parts of the knee.
In joints, hyaline cartilage is also known as articular cartilage. It is the type most commonly damaged by osteoarthritis.
Osteoarthritis can develop as joints experience stress from aging, injury or obesity. Chondrocytes begin producing inflammatory molecules while also breaking down collagen, a structural protein that gives cartilage much of its strength.
As collagen disappears, cartilage becomes thinner and softer. Inflammation adds swelling and pain, creating the familiar symptoms of osteoarthritis.
The problem is that articular cartilage normally has very little ability to repair itself. Researchers have identified possible stem or progenitor cells capable of forming cartilage in bone, but efforts to find similar cell populations within articular cartilage itself have not been successful.
An aging protein becomes a target
Earlier research from Blau's laboratory found that a molecule called prostaglandin E2 is important for the function of muscle stem cells. The protein 15-PGDH breaks down prostaglandin E2.
Blocking 15-PGDH, or otherwise raising levels of prostaglandin E2, has been shown to support regeneration in damaged muscle, nerve, bone, colon, liver and blood cells in young mice.
That raised an important question for Blau, Bhutani and their colleagues: Could the same biological pathway contribute to the deterioration of cartilage as animals age or recover from injury?
The researchers compared 15-PGDH levels in knee cartilage from young and old mice. They found that the amount of the gerozyme roughly doubled with age.
They then gave older animals a small molecule drug designed to inhibit 15-PGDH. In one experiment, the drug was injected into the abdomen so it could have effects throughout the body. In another, it was delivered directly into the knee joint.
Both approaches produced striking results.
Cartilage in the knees of older animals had been noticeably thinner and less functional than cartilage in young mice. After treatment, however, it became thicker across the surface of the joint.
Importantly, the cells were making hyaline cartilage, the smooth articular cartilage needed for healthy joint movement, rather than the less suitable fibrocartilage.
"Cartilage regeneration to such an extent in aged mice took us by surprise," Bhutani said. "The effect was remarkable."
Protecting knees after ACL injuries
The researchers also tested whether the treatment could help after traumatic knee injuries.
ACL tears are particularly common in sports such as soccer, basketball and skiing, where athletes frequently pivot, stop abruptly or jump. Surgery can repair the torn ligament, but fixing the immediate injury does not necessarily prevent long-term joint damage.
About 50% of people who experience these injuries go on to develop osteoarthritis in the affected joint within approximately 15 years.
In the mouse experiments, researchers administered the gerozyme inhibitor twice a week for four weeks after injury. The treatment dramatically reduced the likelihood that the animals would develop osteoarthritis.
Mice that received a control drug had 15-PGDH levels twice those of animals whose knees had not been injured, and they developed osteoarthritis within four weeks.
The treated mice also moved more normally and placed more weight on the paw attached to the injured leg than untreated animals did.
"Interestingly, prostaglandin E2 has been implicated in inflammation and pain," Blau said. "But this research shows that, at normal biological levels, small increases in prostaglandin E2 can promote regeneration."
Making old cartilage cells act younger

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow student of Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

articles.title_orig: Hidden Beauty: UVM student explores Lake Champlain’s underwater world
articles.title_zh: Hidden Beauty: UVM student explores Lake Champlain’s underwater world
articles.content_orig:
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
Graham Montague, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Vermont, is diving into Lake Champlain to showcase its underwater wonders and sharing his discoveries with thousands of followers online.
"I started doing just for a creative outlet and just to make videos that I wanted to actually see myself," Montague said. "I do this all the time anyways, but I started taking my GoPro with me and just started filming fish underneath the water just for fun."
Since 2023, Montague has been documenting life beneath the surface, highlighting underwater vegetation, shipwrecks, and various fish species. His passion for aquatic exploration began with a backyard stream at the Cuyahoga Valley National Park in northeastern Ohio.
"There's so much cool things to see underneath water, but if you're not actually in the water, you're not going to be able to see them," Montague said. "To highlight the beauty of the underwater species is super fun. And it also just gets me outside."
Montague’s academic work focuses on natural resources, aquatic ecology, and fisheries. His current research at UVM examines Lake Champlain’s distinct basins, each with unique environments and fish populations, and tracks how stocked Atlantic salmon move between them.
"We've been tracking them for a couple of years now, and we're finding that Atlantic salmon are moving very far distances throughout the lake and even potentially out of the lake, which is super cool," Montague said.
Between his research and social media videos, Montague hopes to inspire others to explore and protect nature, whether in their own backyard or beneath the surface of a lake.
"The backyard stream in your backyard is going to have a lot of cool fish and wildlife too. That also needs to be conserved and protected and love," Montague said. "So just get outside, enjoy nature, and really just follow what you're passionate about."
Montague’s work demonstrates that you don’t have to look far, or stay above the surface to find something worth protecting.

Purina Institute will join WSAVA Congress in Poland to help veterinary teams turn trusted nutrition science into practical support for clients and their pets
ST. LOUIS , Oct. 6, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Purina Institute will join veterinary professionals from around the world at the 51st World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) Congress in Warsaw, Poland, taking place 13–15 October 2026. As an ongoing Diamond Partner of WSAVA, Purina Institute will support the congress through its sponsored "Food for Thought" educational stream including eight globally renowned speakers, and as the sole sponsor of the WSAVA Global State of Companion Animal Veterinary Practice Report 2026, which will launch during the event.
At WSAVA 2026, delivered in partnership with the Polish Small Animal Veterinary Association (PSAVA) and the Federation of European Companion Animal Veterinary Associations (FECAVA), Purina Institute's sponsored "Food for Thought" stream will highlight the role of nutrition in veterinary care, with presentations on hot topics including canine atopic dermatitis, antimicrobial stewardship and feline kidney disease.
"The WSAVA World Congress offers an important opportunity to listen, learn and share science that can make a difference in everyday veterinary practice," said Dr Marianne Lomberg, Head of Purina Institute. "Through our ongoing partnership with WSAVA, we are helping make nutrition knowledge more accessible and actionable so veterinary teams can support healthier, longer lives for pets."
Beyond the congress, Purina Institute supports several WSAVA committees and initiatives that help veterinary teams apply science in practice. This includes contributing to work with the Nutrition, Education, Animal Welfare and Wellness Committees, as well as work related to One Health and Therapeutics Committees. The Purina Institute also supports strategic WSAVA initiatives through regional Continuing Education events, the annual webinar series and the WSAVA Nutrition Guidelines Course.
Purina Institute believes science is more powerful when it is shared. Its partnership with WSAVA reflects a shared goal: translating trusted, evidence-based nutrition science into practical guidance that empowers veterinary teams to put nutrition at the center of pet health discussions.
For more information about the Purina Institute, visit PurinaInstitute.com .

The World Health Organization says a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia presents a “very low” risk outside the country as investigators look into what caused the death from pneumonia of a lab employee there last week.
The U.N. health agency said on Tuesday that it has been in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The case and the investigation, led by Russian officials, have revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab. WHO has not provided a definitive answer to how the pandemic began.
Here's what to know about the case and how experts are mobilizing after the woman's death:
Pneumonic plague is a form of the disease that affects the lungs
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — which means lung-based and is the most virulent form of the disease — can be as short as 24 hours, according to WHO. It’s a less common but severe form that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time — within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms, WHO says.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often involving the coughing up of blood.
The more common form of plague — bubonic plague — is caused by the bite of an infected flea, and can develop into open sores filled with pus.
Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that is mostly caused by viruses or bacteria, and is spread generally through contact with infected people or from airborne droplets. WHO says pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
A look at what Russian officials are saying about the case
Through an international health alert system, Russian health officials on Tuesday said a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the deceased woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” said the note from Russian authorities, which was relayed to The Associated Press by WHO.
"Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded," it said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”
The woman died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside the city of Irkutsk, and its mayor said the hospital was placed under quarantine. The top officials from Russia’s national public health watchdog traveled to the region on Friday.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov advised the public to follow official statements from the watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
WHO has mobilized its own experts to look into the case
WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told a U.N. briefing on Tuesday that the institute where the woman worked “studies dangerous pathogens,” including plague in a part of Siberia where the disease "occurs naturally in wild animals.”
He said Russian officials have not yet asked for WHO experts to deploy to Russia, where authorities are "looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”
In recent days, WHO has brought in technical experts to its Geneva headquarters and the European regional office in Copenhagen in connection with the investigation, including specialists in high-threat pathogens.
“The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates ... the risk to be moderate-to-low for Irkutsk; a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole; and very low for the WHO European region,” Lindmeier said.
Trump and Rubio have commented on the case
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he was watching the situation with concern and that the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case.
Asked about Trump’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Tuesday that “it is always very good when mutual assistance is offered.” He wouldn’t elaborate further, deferring to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russian authorities to share more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” he said at a news conference in Iceland. “We’re watching it very closely and I think the whole world is watching it very closely."
“We encourage Russia to be more transparent and share more information with the world,” Rubio said, adding this has so far been “quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.”
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, its potential was limited.
Dr. Glenn Wortmann, at the MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said the bacteria that cause plague don't “travel very far” and a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.
“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” he added.
Associated Press writers Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Matthew Lee in Reykjavik, Iceland, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title_orig: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.title_zh: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.content_orig:
From the latest big breakthrough to the most influential and inspiring figures on campus to Pitt in the community, Pittwire is your official source for what’s happening now.
Kati Csoman was still an undergraduate at the University of Pittsburgh when she lived in Hungary for the first time.
She spent the summer of 1988 in the rural northeastern village where her father had grown up. She slept in cousins’ homes, some of which didn’t have indoor plumbing. She picked up Hungarian with a village accent and, for the first time in her life, the language she heard at her childhood kitchen table became something she could speak back.
The immersion into this experience came courtesy of a Nationality Rooms scholarship .
“It really helped me to connect to that part of my life, which is so deeply a part of me,” she says. Three years later, she arrived back in Budapest on a state department fellowship to the U.S. embassy, watching firsthand how Hungary would remake itself after her father’s country voted in its first free elections since the 1940s.
“But, also, it totally changed my academic trajectory and then changed my professional trajectory, too.”
The scholarship launched Csoman (A&S ’89, SPIA ’96G) on a career in international education and connected her not only to her family’s history but also to a broader appreciation of ethnic communities and cross-cultural experiences.
And, eventually, it would lead her back to where it all began.
Today, Csoman is director of Pitt’s Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs, home to 31 spaces inside the Cathedral of Learning that represent the cultural heritages of many of Pittsburgh’s international communities.
The rooms were first imagined in the mid-1920s by Chancellor John Bowman, who wanted a celebration of Pittsburgh’s multicultural presence at the heart of his planned Cathedral of Learning . He turned to Ruth Crawford Mitchell, a Pitt sociologist already closely associated with the city’s ethnic communities through her work with second-generation immigrant students. She gave the program its shape at a time when nearly half of Pittsburgh residents were either born abroad or the children of immigrants. Communities could sponsor classrooms in the Cathedral and, once room construction was complete, leftover funds supported scholarships to send Pitt students abroad year after year. [Watch: Pitt's Nationality and Heritage Rooms are also celebrating a centennial this year. ]
Mitchell stepped back from the directorship in 1957. Shepherd Witman, who arrived at Pitt the following year to direct the Office of Cultural and Educational Exchange, oversaw the rooms during a transitional period, while E. Maxine Bruhns would take the reins in 1965. Bruhns led the Nationality Rooms for the next 55 years, when 12 of the 31 rooms were dedicated and scholarship programs were expanded significantly. Bruhns retired in 2020, with Csoman succeeding her the following year.
But the rooms touched Csoman’s own family long before. Her maternal grandfather had given a dime to help build the Cathedral. Csoman’s father later served on the Hungarian Room Committee, and Csoman herself volunteered with it before becoming the program’s director.
Since the late 1940s, the Nationality Rooms program has supported more than 1,800 Pitt undergrads or graduate students with study abroad scholarships, awarding nearly $5 million in funding. Thirty committees, plus the Women’s International Club, still meet; they fundraise and produce intercultural programming for the campus and wider community, and nearly all of the rooms presently serve as active classrooms or gathering places.
From conceptualization to fundraising to dedication, Pittsburgh’s international communities have shaped each of the rooms into a cultural self-portrait. Every room is designed with precise choices about what best represents a community and how it wants to be seen. A century in, the following stories, centered on the Chinese (dedicated 1939) , Italian (1949) , African Heritage (1989) and Philippine (2019) rooms, reveal examples of how these spaces bridge past and present and often reshape a life’s trajectory.
The Chinese community was not on Mitchell’s original list. In her earliest report to Bowman, Mitchell named 14 ethnic groups interested in building rooms; most were Eastern, Central or Southern European.
While the Chinese community was kept small in the United States by the Immigration Act of 1924 and other federal policies, a group of Chinese graduate students at Pitt sought out Bowman anyway. The Chancellor told them that if they could fundraise and form a committee, they could have a room, says Michael Walter, current manager of education programs for the Nationality Rooms. They organized quickly.
City-wide development also had a significant impact on Pittsburgh’s Chinese community at that time.
The city’s Chinatown neighborhood spanned multiple blocks downtown, but ended up physically divided in the 1920s and 1930s by construction of the city’s Boulevard of the Allies. Pittsburgh’s Chinatown district was all but gone in the following decades with residents moving outward.
Still, the Chinese Room became one of the first nine rooms at Pitt to reach completion. The German, Russian, Scottish, Swedish and Early American rooms were dedicated in 1938, while the Chinese, Czechoslovak, Hungarian and Yugoslav rooms came next in 1939.
The Chinese Room was modeled on an 18th-century reception hall in Beijing’s Forbidden City, the imperial palace at the heart of Ming and Qing dynasty rule.
This art installation inside Hillman Library examines a century of Nationality Rooms history. The installation will run through July 2027.
Yuefang Chang, a research associate professor in Pitt’s School of Medicine’s Department of Neurological Surgery, has been involved with the room for more than a decade, chairing the Chinese Room Committee for the past year and a half.
Chang has worked to learn the room’s history herself, noting that “even within the Chinese community, if they didn’t get a chance to go to the University, they just don’t know about its existence here.”
The first time Chang walked into the room, it surprised her. She had expected the colors to look brighter; instead, the dragons and phoenixes had softened over the decades.
But age and history are essential parts of the experience. Each Nationality Room’s design draws on cultural and traditional markers from before 1787 — the year of Pitt’s founding — meaning every room depicts something far older than the present. Decades of classes, holiday open houses and committee gatherings have only deepened that. Time is the point.
The Chinese Room is full of imperial signifiers: a five-clawed dragon on the ceiling (only the imperial dragon has five, a marker of leadership), phoenixes among peony blossoms, Confucius on the east wall and a round table at the center.
Chang’s committee today includes connections to Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia and the broader diaspora. This year, the Chinese Room committee and the John H. Tsui Memorial Scholarship, named for and seeded by a former chair, together will send seven students to China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
“We all have different backgrounds,” Chang says. “I just hope this room will bring everybody together.”
On the steps of Florence’s Basilica of Santa Maria Novella, Lina Insana (A&S ’91, ’95G) sits with her students and reads from Giovanni Boccaccio’s “The Decameron,” which opens with 10 young Florentines gathered on those same steps in 1348, fleeing the Black Death.
“It was a wonderful way to read that together in a classroom that wasn’t a classroom at all,” she says. Insana, an associate professor of Italian in the Kenneth P. Dietrich School of Arts and Sciences, has taken students to Italy numerous times. She also knows what a Nationality Rooms scholarship makes possible.

articles.title_orig: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.title_zh: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.content_orig:
A pumpkin grower has set a new world record after producing a giant squash.
Ian Paton, from Lymington, Hampshire, entered his exceptionally large specimen into a giant vegetable weigh-off near Reading in Berkshire.
It weighed 2,856.8lbs (1,295.8kg), has circumference of over 20ft (6m) and was officially confirmed by Guinness World Records judge, Sebastian Suski.
Paton said growing the pumpkin named Bagheera, tending to it for up to six hours and providing about 130 gallons of water daily, had been "bloody hard work". It was the first time the 65-year-old, who has grown giant pumpkins with his twin brother Stuart for over 50 years, had entered the competition on his own.
The pumpkin is now on show at Sunnyfields farm near Southampton, where it will be displayed for the next few weeks.
The farm has used more than 10,000 pumpkins and squashes to create a giant pumpkin mural of Sir David Attenborough .
Paton said the pumpkin would later be used as feed for cows.

articles.title_orig: New York declares measles disaster emergency as cases surge in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: New York declares measles disaster emergency as cases surge in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Officials are warning some travelers may have been exposed to measles at select areas inside the Philadelphia International Airport as cases rise in Pennsylvania.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak spreading from Pennsylvania.
It is the first time an emergency declaration has been issued since measles began surging in the U.S. in 2025.
Pennsylvania has reported 977 measles cases and five deaths as of Oct. 2, with most cases centered in rural communities. Meanwhile, New York has reported 108 cases.
WORLD’S MOST CONTAGIOUS VIRUS HITS MAJOR US AIRPORT AS OFFICIALS WARN OF POSSIBLE EXPOSURE
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, speaks during a public safety announcement in New York on Friday, Jan. 30, 2026. (Angelina Katsanis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The U.S. is having its worst year for measles since 1991 , with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
PENNSYLVANIA COMMISSIONER ACCUSES SHAPIRO OF 'DECEPTIVE' MEASLES DEATH FRAMING AS RFK JR BLASTS DEM GOVERNOR
Hochul also issued an executive order expanding the number of health professionals who are approved to administer measles vaccines.
A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center, where the state health department confirmed that a baby tested positive and that there is a possibility of exposure to others at the facility, in New Hyde Park, New York, on March 14, 2025. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)
The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as 2. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults’ consent for such reporting.
DOCTOR SHORTAGES ARE HURTING RURAL PATIENTS. LET PHARMACISTS HELP THEM HEAL
The Pennsylvania and Philadelphia health departments, as well as the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, reported last month that they are "working closely to ensure potentially exposed infants receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles" amid the outbreak.
Sherry Andrews, right, holds 13-month-old Jaqi Herrera’s hand after administering the first MMR vaccine dose to Herrera at the City of Lubbock Health Department in Lubbock, Texas, on February 27, 2025. (Reuters)
Philadelphia Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson wrote that measles exposures are "a reminder of how important it is for all of us to be up to date on our vaccinations ."
MEASLES DEATHS MAY HAVE BEEN 'FABRICATED,' RFK JR CLAIMS AFTER CORONER RAISES QUESTIONS
The health department advised that anyone who has been exposed who is not immune, is unsure of their vaccination status, is an infant, is pregnant and not immune, or is immunocompromised should contact their doctor.
Girl gets checked by a doctor for measles. (iStock)
"Some people may still be eligible for treatment after exposure that can prevent measles or reduce the severity of illness," the department wrote. "Anyone who develops symptoms should call ahead before visiting a healthcare facility and tell the provider about the possible measles exposure."

articles.title_orig: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
articles.title_zh: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has approved the death by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army officer convicted of carrying out a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, an army base in Texas.
The move, if it proceeds, will revive executions in the army, which has not carried one out since 1961.
Death sentences, as well as executions in the US military, are rare and require presidential approval.
Under the army’s code of military justice, premeditated murder does carry the death penalty, but the process is often strict and prolonged.
However, the Trump administration has shown more willingness to seek death penalties for serious crimes, including against civilians.
Here’s what we know about the case:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had initially recommended an execution order for Hasan, and Trump has now approved it, according to an X statement posted by Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.
Parnell said the time and date of the execution will be set by Army Secretary Adam Telle, who is serving in an acting capacity.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” he wrote.
On November 5, 2009, the US-born army major, Hasan, a psychiatrist in the force, walked into an army processing centre in Fort Hood, shouted “Allahu Akbar” (God is great) and opened fire on fellow staff members waiting to get medical attention.
Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier, and 32 others were wounded during 10 minutes of shooting. Analysts have called it the worst shooting at a US military base targeting members of armed forces.
Hasan was shot several times after two officers engaged him and remains paralysed from the waist down.
Hasan was immediately court-martialled, and military prosecutors, from the start, sought the death penalty against him.
However, the process would play out over the course of several years even after his conviction – largely because the US military is averse to capital punishment.
During the trial, Hasan represented himself and admitted to the attacks, saying he was trying to stop deployments to Afghanistan and the killing of his fellow Muslims. He was due to be deployed weeks later.
Investigations revealed Hasan had exchanged emails with Yemeni-American scholar Anwar al-Awlaki, accused of ties to al-Qaeda, before the shooting. He had also repeatedly voiced opposition to the US wars in Iraq and Afghanistan to colleagues and the treatment of Muslims in the army.
Hasan made little effort to defend himself, and his assigned lawyers claimed his testimony aided the opposing side.
He was charged and convicted on 13 counts of premeditated murder in 2013, and jurors recommended the maximum sentence of death. Controversially, Hasan was charged with “workplace violence” because the military justice code does not address the crime of “terrorism”.
The judgement was further delayed by appeals mandated by the military, not because Hasan sought them.
In 2020, the US Army Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the death penalty for Hasan, and in 2023, the US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces did the same. In March 2025, the US Supreme Court denied a mandatory petition for a judicial review.
In September 2025, Hegseth announced he was seeking presidential approval for Hasan’s execution.
At the time, there was no report of Hegseth specifically seeking death by firing squad.
The president holds the ultimate authority to specify the designated method of execution.
Other forms of execution could have been lethal injection or hanging, which the US military has used in the past.
While Trump’s approval will begin a series of steps towards preparing for the execution, Hasan can still put the process on hold for years with an appeal in the civilian federal court system.
However, that might be unlikely as Hasan made no effort to defend himself during the trial.
He has been remanded to the US Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas, where three other men have also been on the military death row for years.
Among them is Hasan Akbar, convicted of two counts of murder after attacking fellow army members on a Kuwait base in 2003, during the invasion of Iraq.
Another is the convicted serial killer and rapist Ronald Gray, who was found guilty of four counts of murder and eight counts of rape in 2008. He was approved for execution in the same year under President George W Bush, but the process was put on hold by a judge.
Timothy Hennis, a former sergeant, was convicted in 2010 of a triple murder and is also on death row.
The last military execution took place in 1961, when former soldier John Bennett was hanged for the rape of an 11-year-old girl.

articles.title_orig: Chapel Intern gains global finance experience at World Bank Treasury
articles.title_zh: Chapel Intern gains global finance experience at World Bank Treasury
articles.content_orig:
Daniel Garcia Calao spent the summer gaining experience in global finance through a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury in Washington, D.C. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — When Daniel Garcia Calao came to Penn State from Bogotá, Colombia, he hoped earning a college degree in the United States would open new opportunities. Four years later, his Penn State journey has taken him from Penn State Abington to Penn State University Park and, most recently, to Washington, D.C., for a summer internship with World Bank Treasury.
Garcia Calao, who is dual majoring in economics and finance with a minor in supply chain and information systems , spent the summer completing a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury . There, he worked with three teams, gaining experience in pensions, asset and liability operations, and advisory services.
“It was a truly global experience that strengthened both my technical skill set and my understanding of international financial institutions,” Garcia Calao said.
As a Chapel Executive Intern , Garcia Calao received enrichment funding through the Liberal Arts Career Enrichment Network to help cover his housing expenses in Washington. He also enrolled in LA 495 Undergraduate Field Experience, a half-credit course designed to help students reflect on and make the most of their internship experiences.
“The Chapel Executive Internship made the summer possible,” Garcia Calao said. “The funding covered my summer housing, which allowed me to save and invest my money and work toward my financial future.”
Garcia Calao was born and raised in Colombia and began his Penn State experience at the Abington campus. As an international student adjusting to a new environment, he found community through campus involvement, eventually serving as president of the Latine Student Organization and participating in student government and Lion Ambassadors .
After two years, he transitioned to the University Park campus, where he continued building his network and pursuing leadership opportunities.
Garcia Calao’s interest in economics and finance continued to grow as he progressed through Penn State. He added economics as a second major to broaden his knowledge and strengthen his preparation for internships and a career in finance. Courses in microeconomics, statistics and environmental economics gave him experience with concepts that he later encountered at World Bank Treasury, including central banking, economic policy and how different economies operate.
Daniel Garcia Calao explored Washington, D.C., while living and working in the city as a Chapel Executive Intern during summer 2026. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Networking also played a major role in helping Garcia Calao find his internship. His path to the World Bank began after attending a Penn State Global Careers Institute event where a Penn State alumnus who worked at the World Bank spoke.
Garcia Calao reached out to the alumnus after the event to learn more, and that conversation helped introduce him to an organization where he had never pictured himself working.
“The whole reason I applied to the World Bank was because of that event,” Garcia Calao said. “Attend events because you never know what opportunities will arise. I wouldn’t have seen myself working at the World Bank before that.”
After getting an interview, Garcia Calao continued using networking to prepare. He reached out to professionals through LinkedIn, including one connection who eventually became a mentor. Those conversations helped him prepare for his interview, better understand the World Bank and think about what he wanted to do after graduation.
He said his favorite rotation was in the pensions department. Because he previously completed an investment internship, he was familiar with some of the work and felt he could demonstrate the skills he had developed. He worked on two projects and was able to see how his work continued to progress after his rotation ended.
“Sometimes interns can feel like the work they’re doing isn’t important,” Garcia Calao said. “Seeing how something I worked on progressed showed me that the work I did provided value to the team.”
Garcia Calao said his international background became an asset during an internship that brought him into contact with colleagues from around the world. Fluent in Spanish and Italian, he was able to draw on his language skills and experience navigating different cultures.
“Being able to communicate properly with people across the world is important,” Garcia Calao said.
Daniel Garcia Calao, middle row, fourth from right, joins fellow World Bank Treasury interns following their final capstone presentation. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Thanks to the Chapel Executive Internship Program, Garcia Calao was able to live right in Washington rather than having to find less expensive housing farther away. Living in Washington also gave Garcia Calao the opportunity to experience the city beyond his internship. He stayed in George Washington University housing, managed his daily commute and explored museums and monuments with fellow interns.
Daniel Garcia Calao participates in the D.C. SCORES tournament while living and working in Washington, D.C., during his summer internship. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
After he graduates this fall, Garcia Calao will join the pensions department at the World Bank where he completed part of his internship. He said he also hopes to eventually attend graduate school.

articles.title_orig: World No.1 Jannik Sinner announces end to 2026 season due to knee injury: "I need a course of treatment for my knee"
articles.title_zh: World No.1 Jannik Sinner announces end to 2026 season due to knee injury: "I need a course of treatment for my knee"
articles.content_orig:
World number one men’s tennis player Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.
The five-time Grand Slam winner will “follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee”, Sinner’s team said in a statement on Tuesday.
“The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027. As a result, Jannik will be unable to compete again during the 2026 season.”
Sinner also posted the update on his personal Instagram account, where he recounted ending last year on a high after retaining his ATP Finals title in Turin as he battled past then world number one Carlos Alcaraz.
“But at the moment, I also need to think about my long-term career,” he said in a video posted on Instagram.
“I will do everything possible to get back to 100 percent [and] I hope to see you very, very soon on court again.”
Sinner, 25, has not played since his triumph at the All England ⁠⁠Club, missing the North American hardcourt swing, including the US Open , and the ongoing ATP 500 event in Beijing.
He announced last week that he was withdrawing from the Shanghai Masters , which he won in 2024 after defeating Novak Djokovic in the final.
Now he will also miss the Paris Masters and the ATP Finals in November. Plus, he will not be able to play for Italy, the host nation and three-time defending champion, in the Davis Cup Final 8.
Sinner risks losing the top ranking while he’s out.
But if Sinner does return at the start of next year, he could play the Australian Open – the next Grand Slam – which starts January 17.
He enjoyed a 30-match winning streak this year before his meltdown in a second-round defeat at the French Open amid a Paris heatwave.
Sinner’s main rival missed four and a half months this year due to a right wrist injury.
Meanwhile, Germany’s Alexander Zverev won two of the four Grand Slam titles and is nearing the No 1 ranking.

articles.title_orig: Democrats’ advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Democrats’ advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Capitol stands on Sept. 23 in Washington, D.C. Finn Gomez/Getty Images hide caption
President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices . But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, and voters are blaming him for costs that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around.
As a result, Republicans are likely to pay the price at the ballot box next month. One month out from Election Day, the electoral landscape has shifted even more so in Democrats' direction.
They are favored to win the House, albeit with a fairly narrow majority. The Cook Political Report forecasts a five-to-15-seat net gain for Democrats at this point. That would give them in the range of 220 to 230 seats come January. (218 is needed for a majority.)
The Senate has shifted more dramatically over the last several months. Six seats have moved more in Democrats' direction since June in comparing Cook's ratings from then to now. When the cycle first started, the Senate was a long shot for Democrats. Now, it's within reach.
And that's largely because of the national mood, which is usually the case in midterms. Trump has just a 37% approval rating, according to an average of the polls . That's tied for the lowest pre-midterm approval in the last half century.
The only other president to be that low in that time was George W. Bush in 2006. Back then, Iraq was spiraling into civil war, and Republicans lost both the House and Senate.
Trump is also facing a historic intensity of opposition; 53% in the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll said they strongly disapprove of the job the president is doing, the highest ever recorded in the survey. That's not a great sign for Republicans with Trump insisting that the midterm elections be about him.
As it is, history is unkind to the president's party in midterm elections. They usually lose about two dozen seats in the House and four in the Senate. It's even worse for the party in power when the president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's is now.
There are multiple reasons Democratic gains might be limited, including mid-decade redistricting helping to insulate Republicans, fewer competitive-to-potentially competitive House seats, with most in districts Trump won in 2024, Republicans' campaign spending edge and the unpopularity of the Democratic Party.
That said, the headwinds the GOP is facing are very real.
Economic issues continue to rate as the top problem and most important issue facing the country.
Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy, but the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased costs on many goods and energy.
The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well and regular people struggling. Wealthy Americans are seeing increases in their wealth and stock portfolios, which are dominated by AI companies.
It's a different story for many others. Inflation is outpacing wages, meaning people's paychecks aren't taking them as far. There isn't a lot of turnover in the labor market, so if someone doesn't have a job or is looking to change, it's not an easy thing to do.
Plus, many are turning against AI . In many places, it's driving up utility costs and, along with the rising national debt, is making borrowing more difficult.
All of that is coming at a time when gas prices have skyrocketed because of the Iran war, and interest rates are creeping higher. In trying to tame inflation, the Federal Reserve hiked rates this fall. That makes it more expensive to borrow money and harder to pay for things like houses and cars.
The blame for that sort of thing often gets pointed directly at the White House and the party in power, and right now, that's Trump and Republicans.
An AP/NORC poll released last week , for example, found that 65% said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump's policies than factors outside of his control.
Just 26% said they approved of the job he's doing on the economy.
An NBC News poll from September found that for only the second time in the Trump era, respondents said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on the economy. (Though it was within the margin of error, the movement in the survey was clear.)
The only other time Democrats led on that question was in 2018 – the last midterm year when Trump was president. Democrats won 42 seats and control of the House then.
Add the widely negative views of the economy to the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, discretionary domestic cuts, the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's all firing up Democrats.
An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year.
In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%.
The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller.
The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms.
"Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it."
There are reasons, however.
First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers.
Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels.
A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans.
What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll , ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?"
In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need.
To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains.
With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts.
Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him.
The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers.
But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win.
The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.

articles.title_orig: A World of Music, A Lasting Gift
articles.title_zh: A World of Music, A Lasting Gift
articles.source: The UCLA Herb Alpert School of Music
articles.content_orig:
Alum Matt Hansen and his parents , Erin and Brian Hansen, have just created the Hansen Family Endowment for scholarships to support students studying ethnomusicology or the global music industry.
I met Matt Hansen on the patio of a Santa Monica coffee shop, tucked behind Def Jam Records in repurposed industrial space. He was recently back from one world tour and about to embark on another. “I’m thankful just to be back in LA for a few months,” he said.
Not that Hansen showed any signs of wear. Dressed casually in a black t-shirt, trucker cap and sunglasses, he waves off the offer of shade. “I was going to sit out in the sun this afternoon anyway,” he explains.
Much like his music, Hansen seems almost incapable of inauthenticity. Despite millions of followers on social media, despite headlining sold-out world tours, Hansen seems unconcerned by the trappings of celebrity. If anyone has recognized him (almost a sure bet in this hip, post-industrial space), they aren’t letting on. And Hansen couldn’t seem to care less. He treasures his many fans and followers, who in turn treasure their connection to his deeply emotional and unequivocally honest music. At the same time, he doesn’t really consider himself famous and is careful not to become addicted to the need to be loved.
The endowed scholarship bears the hallmarks of Hansen’s own musical journey. Hansen majored in ethnomusicology, mainly because he loves music from all across the world. “When I’m on tour, I’ll grab three or four records in every record shop. I’ll have no idea what they are, sometimes they will be in different languages, and I’ll bring them home, and I’ll listen to them. I love that discovery.”
Some of that can be chalked up to the Department of Ethnomusicology’s venerable tradition of bi-musicality—the pedagogical practice of teaching music as both theory and practice. Students take classes, but also join performance ensembles on world traditions, from Ghana to Tibet, from Mexico to India. At UCLA, Hansen learned how to play instruments he had never seen before. He studied microtonal progressions. And he learned from masters of the craft who brought varied experiences with music.
“I was really moved by people’s emotional connection to music,” said Hansen. “I played with the Iranian music ensemble, under Pejman Hadadi. He would tell me stories about how hard he worked to keep Iranian musical traditions alive. You could see his passion, his deep love. And all I could think, was—there’s so much to learn from that.”
Given Hansen’s honesty and deep connections to global music, it should not surprise anyone that you can find his fans on every continent. But it sometimes surprises Hansen. He recounted his recent trip to South Africa, where he played the Montreux Jazz Festival . Hansen, who has no record label and who had never been to the country before, couldn’t figure the booking. “I went out on the stage, and I was so confused why they had booked me—no one there would know the music. And I look out in the audience, and people are singing my songs. And the next day, people are walking up to me with the Google Translate app to talk to me about the music.”
Hansen started at UCLA in 2018, and at times wasn’t sure of himself as he started off in a demanding school of music. “I was a little closed off when I arrived. I felt like I needed to fade back, not step on anybody’s toes, and stay in the background. And I didn’t really grasp that the best thing I could do in education was get out of my comfort zone.”
Hansen recalled a pivotal moment when he played with the Afro-Cuban ensemble, where he had to sing in Spanish—a language he barely knew. And while the Matt Hansen of 2026 appears at ease on the stage and the (social media) screen, the same was not true for the student trying out Afro-Cuban music for the first time.
“I said to myself, I’m going to try this, just try it. And there I was, singing in front of everybody. And dancing, too. I mean—dancing was not a thing that I did, ever. But I did it.”
Like many students of that time, COVID upended his life. The disruption, the social distancing—it pushed him off one path and left him uncertain and drifting. Briefly he contemplated leaving school altogether. Ultimately, it led him to the rooftop of Parking Deck 3 on the far northern edge of campus, where he videorecorded himself performing covers at the top of his lungs. He uploaded Frank Ocean’s “ Godspeed ” to TikTok and it went viral. Really viral. Almost overnight, it had tens of millions of views.
Instant fame in the midst of pandemic isolation can prove disorienting. His inbox flooded with interest from record executives. There was pressure to push on. And there were also moments of serendipity, like when Hansen discovered in Fall 2022 that he was trending in Tehran.
“My cover of “Titanium” was being picked up by Iranian influencers and reused. I didn’t know why, I was really confused,” said Hansen. “And I looked at the comments, and they are all in Farsi.”
The people of Iran had taken to the streets to protest the killing of Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish woman who had been beaten by Iran’s morality police for not wearing her hijab in public.
She later died in police custody. The palpable anger of widespread protests—largely spontaneous and leaderless—caught the world’s eye. And Hansen’s cover of “Titanium” became part of the soundtrack of rebellion.
Hansen used the moment to raise money for the Center for Human Rights in Iran . The experience stayed with him throughout the years, making him reflect on what success was, and what it was worth.
After his career in the music industry began to take off, Hansen and his family decided to do something that would have a lasting impact. They endowed a scholarship for students studying ethnomusicology or the global music industry.
“I’ve realized how lucky I was at UCLA, building a foundation of knowledge, meeting a great network of people that I love,” said Hansen, “I want others to be able to have that experience too.”
